component: P1.1 source/text reads and checkout enumeration
constraints: Offline developer scans on Linux/macOS/Windows; Python3.9 compatibility. Preserve complete selected tracked/untracked coverage, generated-directory rules, path checks and visible errors. No frozen file or product threshold edits.
Prevent unbounded input reads and directory queue growth through explicit rejection budgets. Preserve existing AST semantics; no runtime-security, real-time or whole-process memory guarantee.
comparison: Python os.scandir is an incremental iterator with context-managed closure; explicit shared counting rejects excess without collecting complete directory listings or changing existing path/error checks. Buffered read(size) provides bounded returned input for source and other text.

Rust walkdir2.5 offers max_depth/max_open, but max_depth deliberately avoids descending beyond its limit. That default would silently prune required coverage here; an explicit fail-on-excess visitor and shared accounting would still be required. Root symlink handling also needs explicit preservation.

Java DirectoryStream supports incremental enumeration and try-with-resources closure. It remains a credible different-language option, but still needs shared admission counting, explicit depth failure and a boundary to the Python-version-specific AST parser. No Rust/Java performance benchmark was run and no throughput ranking is inferred.
rationale: KEEP Python/native filesystem I/O for this boundary: it supports incremental enumeration and bounded reads in the process that applies Python AST rules, with an executable rejection contract and no extra pathname/content serialization boundary. The defect was absent admission accounting; existing language familiarity is not a reason.

Implement source/text admission v1:1MiB/16MiB per-file/total source,8MiB/64MiB other text,100000 enumerated entries shared across phases,depth64 relative to each scan root. These finite generous developer defaults are not hardware-derived execution guarantees.
